content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studied OOD generalization under the federated learning setting. The author proposes dual-regularization to improve the OOD robustness in FL. Experiments are conducted in three federated datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

+ The problem of OOD generalization in FL is well-motivated.

+ The proposed methods are technically sound with intensive theoretical analysis.

+ Extensive experiments have been conducted to validate the proposed method empirically.
 
Weaknesses:

- Overclaimed innovation. This paper is claimed to be the first to consider and handle the out-of-distribution problem under the Non-IID FL setting. However, several papers tackle the same problem (e.g., [1], [2]). The authors should attenuate their tone a bit.

- Incremental technical contribution. The proposed dual-regularization is incremental. All the mentioned techniques are well-studied in invariance learning and personalized federated learning. The authors failed to justify the technique challenge. For example, it is unclear what are the specific challenges to extending IRM for federated learning.

- Missing fair baseline comparison. Although this paper report results for GroupDRO, there exists a federated version of Group DRO (e.g., DRFA [3], FedRobust [4]). The authors are suggested to report the results of DRFA/FedRobust for a fair comparison.

Typos:

Page 5 (4.1): “.. in each training contexts will make .. ” → “.. in each training context will make .. ” 

Page 6 (line 5): “ nother” → “another” 


References:

[1] Liu, Q., Chen, C., Qin, J., Dou, Q., & Heng, P. A. (2021). Feddg: Federated domain generalization on medical image segmentation via episodic learning in continuous frequency space. In CVPR.

[2] Yuan, H., Morningstar, W. R., Ning, L., & Singhal, K. (2022). What Do We Mean by Generalization in Federated Learning?. In ICLR.

[3] Deng, Y., Kamani, M. M., & Mahdavi, M. (2020). Distributionally robust federated averaging. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 33, 15111-15122.

[4] Reisizadeh, A., Farnia, F., Pedarsani, R., & Jadbabaie, A. (2020). Robust federated learning: The case of affine distribution shifts. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 33, 21554-21565.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper can be further improved regarding clarity and quality. The novelty is incremental regarding the proposed method. The reproducibility is okay since the proposed method is straightforward and technically sound.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper combines IRM and FL to solve the OOD generalization task under the federated setting.
The core idea is to inject dual regularizer to enforce the learned representation with local and global invariance.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Pros
1. The theoretical analysis is comprehensive and insightful.
2. The idea of incorporating IRM into FL by a dual regularizer is novel.

## Cons
1. The experiments have shown that the OOD performance of the proposed method is improved. However, the use of IRM is known to hinder the in-distribution performance. Therefore, the trade-off between OOD and ID performance needs to be discussed. Further, the WaterBirds dataset consists of different subpopulations and is typically used for evaluating the model robustness against subpopulation shift. Therefore, it's better to report both the worst and average performance on this dataset as previous work did [1].
2. There is already  some works focus on combining the distributional robust optimization with FL. DRFA [1,2] is a recent work by imposing adaptive weight to each client. The comparison between the proposed method and the related work needs to be provided.

## Refs
[1]Huaxiu Yao, Yu Wang, Sai Li, Linjun Zhang, Weixin Liang, James Zou, and Chelsea Finn.
Improving out-of-distribution robustness via selective augmentation.
[2] Distributionally Robust Federated Averaging. 
[3] DRFLM: Distributionally Robust Federated Learning with Inter-client Noise via Local Mixup

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper explores the problem of both OOD data (i.e., domain generalization) and client heterogeneity in the federated learning context.
The proposed solution simply solves the global invariant problem and then solves a personalized version for each client.
The paper provides some theory on the convergence of the method under certain assumptions.
Finally, the paper gives empirical evidence for the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
*Strengths*
- The paper addresses two types of data heterogeneity in FL, OOD and client heterogeneity.

- The paper provides a simple solution by solving the global domain generalization problem and then locally training the models to be near this global solution.

- The paper provides empirical evidence on MNIST, FMNIST and a birds dataset that the proposed approach can perform better than some baselines.

*Weaknesses*
- The paper has missed important recent references on domain generalization in the federated setting.  In particular, [FedDG] and [FedADG] and very recently [FedSR]. This last one [FedSR] may be considered a concurrent work but is clrearly relevant and could be at least discussed.  The paper should compare to [FedDG] and [FedADG] and remove claims of being the first ones to consider OOD in the FL setting.

[FedDG] Liu, Q., Chen, C., Qin, J., Dou, Q., & Heng, P. A. (2021). Feddg: Federated domain generalization on medical image segmentation via episodic learning in continuous frequency space. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (pp. 1013-1023).

[FedADG] Zhang, L., Lei, X., Shi, Y., Huang, H., & Chen, C. (2021). Federated learning with domain generalization. arXiv preprint arXiv:2111.10487.

[FedSR] Nguyen, A. T., Lim, S. N., & Torr, P. H. FedSR: Simple and Effective Domain Generalization Method for Federated Learning. Accepted to NeurIPS 2022. https://atuannguyen.com/assets/pdf/NeurIPS_nguyen2022fedsr.pdf

- IRM nor GroupDRO are SOTA in the centralized setting.  See for example the WILDS benchmarks: https://wilds.stanford.edu/leaderboard/ For example, even CORAL can outperform more advanced methods in some cases and should be easy to implement as another baseline. Thus, additional SOTA baselines would improve the paper.

[CORAL] Sun, B., & Saenko, K. (2016, October). Deep coral: Correlation alignment for deep domain adaptation. In European conference on computer vision (pp. 443-450). Springer, Cham.

- The algorithm seems significantly more complex than it needs to be.  The global problem should be solved via FL. Then, the local models can be fit. I did not see any reason why these need to be done at the same time.  This simplifies the algorithm. If there is a reason this must be tied together, then an ablation experiment should be performed. 

- (Minor) The paper lacks any discussion on the communication cost of their method in comparison to other methods.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- Assumption 2 seems strong and possibly unrealistic in practice. Can you provide more explanation of when this could hold or when it will not hold?  Do you have empirical evidence to understand this constant on real-world data?  More generally, a deeper discussion of this assumption seems critical.

- In Algorithm 1, why are the local models updated while the global model is being updated?  The global updates are not dependent on the local models in any way so it could be done independently before solving the personalized models. (see comment below) 

- Initially, equation 2 and 3 seem to form a bilevel optimization problem.  However, there does not seem to be any dependence of (3) on the parameters of (2), so (3) can be solved completely independently of (2).  Is that correct or is some notation missing?

- The paper says the IRM problem can be "naturally decomposed into N subproblems". It is unclear that this naive decomposition will work in the Federated setting. The resulting models could easily diverge and not solve the global objective---which is important for OOD performance. Could you comment on this challenge?

- Assumption 1 is written confusingly and needs to be made more clear.  Particularly the sentence starting with "There are K=pN clients..." What is $p$? What is $N_K$?  Roughly, it seems that (i) corresponds to the idea that there are some features that are unique AND invariant for some of the clients (but possibly not all).

- It seems Assumption 1 assumes that EACH client has a set of training domains.  Is that correct? Why would this be a reasonable assumption? Also, this should probably be a separate assumption or more explicitly explained. This also seems to be assumed in Section 4.  Again, a justification for this assumption is needed.

- Theorem 1 is written oddly since the average over $i$ does not even include $i$. Is that a typo or is it just an average over a constant which is just the constant itself? This theorem also seems to be almost trivially true given the definition of $\Phi_g$ being the intersection and hence a subset of $\Phi_i$, i.e., having more features is always at least not worse than having less features. I'm not sure this theorem is particularly interesting or useful.

- "to solve the challenging OOD problem for every client" -> This claim is overstated and should be significantly softened. This paper makes a step towards solving the OOD problem, but to claim that it solves the problem is too strong.

- "gloal" -> "global" page 1
- "exsiting" -> "existing" page 1
- "disscting" -> "dissect"? page 2
- "learing" -> "learning" page 2
- "Invraint" page 3
- "nother", page 6
- "water background...water background" -- repeated?
- "effecrively extract the invarinat features"
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper presents a simple approach to personalized invariant learning in the federated setting.  First, find an invariant subspace using FL across clients.  Then, train a personalized invariant model on each client.  This assumes that each client has multiple domains. The approach is simple and natural but is a bit conflated with complexity in the algorithm and theory. Also, key related work and baselines were missing.  The results seem better but do not directly give evidence for the assumptions being true or the theory being correct with any clarity.  The paper could be improved by simplifying the overall story and claims, adding necessary baseline methods, and focusing on insights into the problem in the experiments.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a method for addressing client heterogeneity (via personalization) and train/test distributional shift (OOD generalization) simultaneously. They derive an algorithm and prove both convergence results as well as OOD generalization guarantees, and experimentally verify the superior performance over naive methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
- Strong theoretical analysis
- Experimental results suggest the new method is a significant improvement over existing methods.

Weakness
- Assumption 1 seems like a very strong assumption to make. Fortunately it does not seem that anything from this assumption is required to be known in order to set parameters of the algorithm.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper could benefit from the problem formulation being better described at the beginning. In particular it is difficult to understand how the different train/test environments can differ from each other (the definition of invariance seems to implicitly sweep this under the rug, but it would be valuable to clarify this when the concept of environments is introduced), or even how an 'environment' is defined or should be though about. 

Experimental results are quite thorough and compelling. In particular experiments comparing naive OOD learning to the proposed method show the necessity of the complexity of the new method.

content.title: Exploiting Personalized Invariance for Better Out-of-distribution Generalization in Federated Learning
content.TL;DR: We are the first to consider the challenging out-of-distribution generalization problem under Non-IID federated learning setting and propose the novel concept of personalized invariance and method to handle it.
content.abstract: Recently, data heterogeneity among the training datasets on the local clients (a.k.a., Non-IID data) has attracted intense interest in Federated Learning (FL), and many personalized federated learning methods have been proposed to handle it. However, the distribution shift between the training dataset and testing dataset on each client is never considered in FL, despite it being general in real-world scenarios. We notice that the distribution shift (a.k.a., out-of-distribution generalization) problem under Non-IID federated setting becomes rather challenging due to the entanglement between personalized and spurious information. To tackle the above problem, we elaborate a general dual-regularized learning framework to explore the 'personalized invariance', compared with the exsiting personalized federated learning methods which are regularized by a single baseline (usually the global model). Utilizing the personalized invariant features, the developed personalized models can efficiently exploit the most relevant information and meanwhile eliminate spurious information so as to enhance the out-of-distribution generalization performance for each client. Both the theoretical analysis on convergence and OOD generalization performance and the results of extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of our method over the existing federated learning and invariant learning methods, in diverse out-of-distribution and Non-IID data cases.
